How to Write a Sympathy Message: Kind Words for a Difficult Time

Learn how to write a thoughtful sympathy or condolence message. Find simple wording, examples and guidance on what to avoid when someone is grieving.

A helpful sympathy message is usually short, sincere and focused on the person who is grieving. Acknowledge the loss, say that you are thinking of them, and offer specific support only if you can genuinely provide it. You do not need to explain the loss or find perfect words.

Emotional Support8–10 min readUpdated 7 November 2026
Written by RA FahimWishly Guide Editorial

Quick answer

Use the person’s name, acknowledge what happened in plain language, share a brief memory if appropriate and offer one realistic form of support. Keep the message gentle and do not ask the recipient to comfort you or reply.

  • Acknowledge the loss directly and warmly.
  • Avoid clichés, comparisons or explanations about why the loss happened.
  • Offer specific help without making the grieving person responsible for organising it.

Start with a simple acknowledgement

When someone experiences a death, people often delay writing because they are afraid of saying the wrong thing. A direct sentence is enough to begin: “I am so sorry to hear about your father.” You do not have to make the message elaborate or explain how the person should feel.

Use the relationship and context to guide your tone. A note to a close friend may be warmer and more personal than a message to a colleague. If you did not know the person who died, you can still express care for the person who is grieving.

Add a memory or meaningful detail when appropriate

If you knew the person who died, a brief memory can make the message feel personal. Mention a quality you admired, a moment you shared or something they taught you. Keep it true and avoid turning the note into a long story that the recipient may not have the energy to read.

If you did not know them, do not invent a connection. Focus on the recipient: “I know how much your grandmother meant to you. I am thinking of you and your family.” Honesty is kinder than pretending to know more than you do.

Offer practical help without creating pressure

General offers such as “Let me know if you need anything” are well-intentioned, but someone who is grieving may not know what to ask for. If you are able, offer one specific action: bringing a meal, collecting groceries, making a phone call or helping with a practical task. Make it easy to decline.

Only offer help you can genuinely deliver. Do not promise daily support if your schedule cannot sustain it. A simple message that leaves room for the person’s choice is better than a large promise that later disappears.

  • “I can drop dinner at your door on Thursday if that would help.”
  • “I am free to handle the school pickup tomorrow. Would you like me to?”
  • “No need to reply. I just wanted you to know I am thinking of you.”

Know what to avoid saying

Avoid phrases that minimise grief or try to explain it, such as “Everything happens for a reason,” “At least they lived a long life” or “I know exactly how you feel.” Even when intended as comfort, these statements can make someone feel that their loss is being compared, corrected or rushed.

You also do not need to ask for details about the death unless the person chooses to share them. Respect cultural, religious and family differences. If you are unsure what is appropriate, choose a simple message that acknowledges the person and offers care.

Examples for different relationships

For a close friend: “I am heartbroken to hear about your loss. I remember how warmly you spoke about your mother. I am here to listen, sit with you or help with something practical whenever you want.”

For a colleague: “I am very sorry for your loss. Please accept my condolences. Wishing you and your family care and support during this difficult time.” For someone you do not know well, keep the message brief and respectful.

Follow up with care after the first message

People often receive many messages immediately after a loss and may hear from fewer people later. A gentle follow-up after some time can help: “I was thinking of you today. Would a short call or a quiet visit be helpful this week?” Do not treat a lack of reply as rejection.

Grief does not follow a fixed timeline. Continue to respect the person’s preferences, privacy and energy. Your role is not to remove their sadness; it is to offer steady, considerate support without demanding a particular response.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good short sympathy message?

“I am so sorry for your loss. I am thinking of you and your family. There is no need to reply, but I am here if you would like support.”

What should I write in a sympathy card?

Acknowledge the loss, share a brief sincere thought or memory if appropriate, and offer support you can genuinely provide.

Is it okay to send condolences by text?

Yes, especially when a text is the most appropriate or accessible way to reach the person. Keep it respectful and do not expect an immediate response.

What should I avoid saying to someone who is grieving?

Avoid minimising the loss, explaining why it happened, comparing grief or saying you know exactly how the person feels. Listen and follow their lead.
